sections.body: The AI Physician is the part of this atlas that follows artificial intelligence into medical work, from reading scans to drafting notes to sorting molecules. In practice, the field is less about a machine replacing a doctor and more about narrow systems that classify images, flag anomalies, predict deterioration, transcribe conversations, and search genomic patterns. This atlas currently tracks 1000 medical AI models, which gives a sense of how many separate tools and research systems are now in circulation. These systems appear in radiology queues, pathology slides, intensive care monitors, drug discovery pipelines, and remote triage services. They are also embedded in surgical navigation, population health dashboards, brain mapping, and the security layers around connected medical devices. The work is real and deployed, but it is uneven, and most systems remain assistants or second readers rather than autonomous clinicians.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Where the work stands is mixed. Imaging has some of the clearest evidence, with models that match or exceed specialist performance on narrow detection tasks, yet they still struggle with rare findings, different scanners, and messy real world data. Genomics and drug discovery have produced useful predictions and candidate molecules, but turning those into approved treatments remains slow and expensive. Clinical documentation and ambient intelligence have moved quickly into routine use, though accuracy, privacy, and clinician trust remain open problems. Intensive care and predictive analytics can warn about deterioration, but alerts often add noise, and the evidence that they change patient outcomes is not uniform. The atlas records 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that accountability is now part of the technical story. Regulation, device security, and post market monitoring are not solved, and no serious observer claims that medical AI is finished.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section are arranged by clinical and technical domain rather than by product. A reader who wants the most mature evidence should start with Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology, then move to Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics for the data heavy side of diagnosis and treatment matching. Clinical Documentation and Ambient Intelligence covers the administrative and conversational tools that are already changing daily practice, while Surgical Robotics and Navigation and Predictive Patient Analytics and Intensive Care show AI in the operating room and at the bedside. Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation and Telemedicine and Triage address the pipeline before treatment and the front door of care, and Epidemiology and Population Health widens the view to groups and systems. Neuroinformatics and the Brain handles the most complex organ and the research tools built around it, and Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security closes the loop with the rules, risks, and protections that surround every other page. The atlas holds 215 compliance and regulation pages, so that final area is not a footnote but a substantial part of the map.
